Unit 1
 Verb Mood
 Part A Indicative and Imperative
 Preview
 Class Notice
 There will be no computer class tomorrow as
 we are upgrading the computer server. The
 new server is bigger and faster than the previous
 one. The classroom door will be locked all day,
 so do not attempt to enter. Use the time for
 your private study and remember to collect
 your new log-in password. Send me your email
 address so I can give you some homework. The
 work must be finished by Friday.
 Grammar Explanation
 Verb Moods: Indicative and Imperative
 The indicative mood is the most common verb mood in English. It is used to express facts and opinions,
 or to ask questions about them. The indicative mood is used in all verb tenses.
 Indicative Conjugation (Simple Present): I am going to visit Paris next week.
 am You looked happy yesterday.
 I My dog is barking at passing cars.
 walk
 is Does she have my book?
 He / She / It Do they study English on Tuesdays?
 walks
 are
 You / We / They
 walk
 The imperative mood is used to make requests or give orders and warnings. It is used only in the
 simple present and future tenses.
 The subject in the imperative mood is always Pass me the salt, please.
 you. In simple present tense, the you-subject is Don’t walk near my vegetable garden.
 not usually stated. Look out for those bees!
 In the simple future tense, the you-subject is Finish your homework tonight. (command)
 usually stated. It is used to place stronger You will finish your homework tonight!
 emphasis on a command. (strong command)

 Part A 9
 Part B Present Subjunctive
 Preview
 Principal: I am recommending that Mrs.
 Robinson stay home until after her
 baby is born.
 Jenny: When is her baby due?
 Principal: Around September 15th. I requested
 that she return to school in January.
 Mark: Who is going to teach us until then?
 Principal: Ms. Shaw. I insist you be as respectful
 to her as you are to Mrs. Robinson!
 Grammar Explanation
 The subjunctive mood is used to express uncertain actions or states.
 The present subjunctive* is formed with the base form of a verb. It follows verbs, nouns, or adjectives
 that express suggestion, demand, or request.
 Words of suggestion used: determine, The doctor suggested I sleep more.
 determination, propose, recommend, My recommendation is that he sleep more.
 recommendation, suggest, suggestion, The doctor’s recommendation is that they sleep more.
 advise, advisable, critical, desirable, It is advisable that she sleep more.**
 important, vital, urge
 Words of demand used: demand, My parents demand that I be quiet at night.
 imperative, insist, necessary, order, Your parents require that you be quiet at night.
 require, required It is imperative that she not be noisy at night.
 Words of request used: ask, beg, prefer, I ask that you have more patience with the other students.
 request, wish The teacher requested that Nick have his project finished
 a day earlier.
 * The term “present” refers to the form of the subjunctive verb (base form) rather than the time in
 which the action happens. The following sentences all use the present subjunctive mood:
 The patient asked that he be given more medicine.
 The patient requests that he be given more medicine.
 The patient is demanding that he be given more medicine.
 The patient will insist that he be given more medicine.
 ** Often, that is not omitted from sentences.

 Part B 13
 Part C Past Subjunctive
 Preview
 Dear friends,
 I’m having a great time here in Canada. So far, I
 have been skiing, ice skating, and fishing. It looks
 as if it’s going to be sunny tomorrow, so we might
 even go camping! There’s so much to do. If I were
 back home, I would never have done all these fun
 things. I wish you were all here with me. If only
 you weren’t so busy, you could join me. Well,
 hope to see you soon.
 Your friend,
 Claire
 Grammar Explanation
 The subjunctive mood is also used to express uncertain actions or states.
 The past subjunctive* is formed with the simple past form of a verb that describes a state, condition,
 or habit. With the verb be, the form were (not was) is always used. It refers to hypothetical or imaginary
 situations.
 The past subjunctive is used after the verb I wish Sally were here to help us.
 wish to express an unfulfilled desire. He wishes he could run faster.
 It is also used after the verbs suppose and Suppose you met the president. What would you say?
 imagine or with if (only) phrases to express Imagine you were rich. What would you do first?
 unreal conditions. Such sentences are usually If people drove smaller cars, we could all breathe
 followed by would or could. cleaner air.
 The past subjunctive is also used when a She acts as though she were very rich, but she’s not.
 comparison to an imaginary condition is He drives as if he were in a Formula 1 race.
 made. In this case, as though or as if
 usually precedes it.
 * The term “past” refers to the form of the subjunctive verb (past simple) rather than the time in which
 the action happens. The following sentences all use the past subjunctive mood:
 If I were more organized, I would have arrived yesterday.
 If I were you, I would call her right now.
 If I weren’t sick, I would go skiing with you tomorrow.
